newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania presidential election too close to call.
newsitem.headline: Romania presidential election too close to call.

text.p: Romanians voted on Sunday in a close run-off contest that could end President Ion Iliescu's seven years in power and symbolically finish the 1989 anti-communist revolt.
Iliescu, a senior official under dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, is running neck-and-neck with Emil Constantinescu, an academic who held no office under communism.
Voters gave Iliescu a small lead over Constantinescu in the first round, but threw his leftist party out of government for the first time since the bloody 1989 overthrow of Ceausescu.

The opposition says leftists hijacked the 1989 revolution to seize power. They say the election can end Romania's status as the one Eastern European country where anti-communists have not held power and finally improve the country's image abroad.
Seeking support amongst pensioners and peasants Constantinescu attended an Orthodox service at the ornate Casin monastery and was cheered on by hundreds of supporters when he voted with his family.
"If I am elected, I will not only be a new president but a different kind of president," he said. "A president who will stay in touch with ordinary Romanians."

There were no reliable opinion polls between the two rounds and the results will be close. Exit polls will give the first indication after polling ends at midnight (2200 gmt). Official results will trickle in on Monday.
Constantinescu, a geology professor, accuses Iliescu of seven years of corrupt mismanagement that has left Romanians in poverty with average monthly salaries of less than $100.

The president vowed during the campaign to shield Romanians against the excesses of market economics and told voters his rival would restore exiled King Michael and pre-war landlords bent on reclaiming their homes and closing factories.
"I believe I can be the best alternative in the present situation. A president needs experience," he said after chatting to voters outside a Bucharest polling station.
"I can ensure cooperation between the opposition and the government in the country's best interests. I am prepared for any alternative. I am a realistic politician and a fighter."
Constantinescu has won the backing of most political parties, including Iliescu's first post-1989 prime minister Petre Roman, who came third in the opening round.
He may also benefit from the negative campaigning style of the 66-year-old president who has reportedly been worn out by the election struggle.
If he hangs on for another term, Iliescu will faces a hostile cabinet demanding faster change to bridge the gap in living standards with near neighbours Hungary and Poland.
A new government dominated by Constantinescu's centrist Democratic Convention will be formed within days.
Iliescu needs a big turnout in rural areas, where he is backed solidly by less educated voters fearing change.
Officials said early turnout was as high as in the first round with some 10 percent voting in the first four hours.

"I voted for Emil. We need change," said one elderly woman outside a suburban Bucharest polling station. "We've seen change all around us but not in Romania. We've started to worry that it won't happen here."
Most voters queried in one of the impoverished villages southeast of the capital said they had backed Iliescu.
First round voting was marked by confusion over outdated voters lists but international observers pronounced the ballot generally free and fair.
